item.title: Mike Tomlin calls Steelers situation following Aaron Rodgers vs. Mike McCarthy feud 'a dumpster fire'
item.description: Mike Tomlin calls the Steelers situation following the Aaron Rodgers vs. Mike McCarthy feud a "dumpster fire" and admits he's sad and upset.
item.content:encoded:
Mike Tomlin coached the Pittsburgh Steelers for 19 years, and although there was a Super Bowl high and that low earlier this year when he decided to quit, he never presided over something like the Aaron Rodgers vs. Mike McCarthy feud going public the past couple of days.

And Tomlin didn't like it. He said the prevailing feeling about the situation now is "just general sadness."

And worse.

SUPER BOWL-WINNING COACH MIKE TOMLIN LANDS NBC ROLE ON 'FOOTBALL NIGHT IN AMERICA' BROADCAST

"I'm upset about it," Tomlin said during a halftime interview with play-by-play voice Mike Tirico on NBC's Sunday Night Football broadcast. "Um, you know, it's a dumpster fire. And I don't say that in a judgmental way.

"I've presided over a few dumpster fires in my 19 years. But it certainly is upsetting, and I'm sure, Steelers nation is upset."

AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY DISAGREEMENTS AT HEART OF QUARTERBACK'S BENCHING BY THE STEELERS

On Tuesday the Steelers announced they were benching Rodgers and making him inactive for Friday's game against the Denver Broncos.

On Wednesday, Rodgers responded by going on the "Pat McAfee Show" and claiming McCarthy falls asleep in meetings, snores in those meetings, isn't prepared with the game play as late as Tuesday, misstated what team he coaches while breaking down the team at halftime of a game against the Philadelphia Eagles, and is generally "unwell."

Within hours, the Steelers released Rodgers. McCarthy denied falling asleep and missing meetings, and accused Rodgers of presenting him with "an ultimatum" about taking the play-calling away from the coach or he'd ask to be released – something Rodgers confirmed.

AARON RODGERS NFL CAREER SEEMS OVER BUT THREE TEAMS COULD CONSIDER QUARTERBACK AS A LATE-SEASON OPTION

"I had a range of emotions watching those course of events play out yesterday," said Tomlin, who coached the Steelers from 2007 through last season. "I think the prevailing [feeling] is just general sadness. Sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career of the quarterback, Aaron Rodgers.

"And just on the macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum. Those are things that kind of run counter-culture to professional football."

Tomlin coached Rodgers last season and it is no secret he respected and admired Rodgers for year before that. That's one reason the Steelers were interested in signing Rodgers last season.

But Tomlin said it nonetheless shocked him when Rodgers pulled back the curtain on his feelings for McCarthy on national TV.

"It certainly did," Tomlin said. "But, you know, particularly because I know both men involved. Certainly had a lot of intimate work and and development of relationship with Aaron over the last couple of years and have known and competed against Mike, you know, respected and appreciated him as a coach for a long time."

There has been no Steelers player that either publicly or privately has said what Rodgers said untrue. Tomlin was asked how the quarterback is viewed in the Steelers locker room.

"He was beloved, and I'm not, you know, over-exaggerating that," Tomlin said. "He worked at it, and people appreciated his openness to getting to know and understand the Steeler culture, to be engaged with teammates."

How?

"Particularly from my perspective, I worked with a lot of veteran players over the years, and at times, they lose a little patience for the process," Tomlin said. "Or they lose patience for relationships with younger guys.

"Man, he seemed to embrace all of that and really embrace it in a real natural way."

STEELERS TEAM PRESIDENT CHOOSES SIDE IN AARON RODGERS, MIKE MCCARTHY SPLIT

So does Tomlin believe McCarthy can effectively lead the Steelers the rest of the way this season after what Rodgers uncovered?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

And here's a hint to his answer: It's not a definitive yes.

"You know, it certainly created some challenges and challenges is probably an understatement if all of those things are true," Tomlin said. "...But his ability to overcome that, or inability to overcome that, in my opinion, is based on relationships."

That is an unvarnished view of the situation from someone who lived within that Steelers organization and culture for nearly two decades.

It doesn't suggest the Steelers are going to be fine.

item.title: Strobe Talbott, former deputy secretary of state and Brookings Institution president, dies at 80
item.description: Strobe Talbott, the former deputy secretary of state who advised Bill Clinton on Russian affairs and led the Brookings Institution, has died at 80.
item.content:encoded:
Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state whose deep expertise on the Soviet Union shaped U.S. foreign policy before he went on to lead the Brookings Institution, died Thursday at the age of 80.

Talbott’s son, Devin Talbott, said his father died peacefully after a long illness at his home in East Hampton, New York, The Associated Press reported.

An Ohio native, Talbott began his journalism career as an intern at Time magazine while studying at Yale and Oxford, where he was roommates with future President Bill Clinton. Clinton later joked that his job in their shared apartment was to make Talbott breakfast every morning.

NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

While at Time, Talbott was tapped to translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former Soviet leader ousted in 1964, which earned him a full-time role at the magazine.

Over a 21-year career there, he focused on U.S.-Soviet relations, led the Washington bureau, and wrote as a foreign affairs columnist.

In 1994, Talbott joined the Clinton administration as deputy secretary of state, helping guide U.S. relations with Russia and other post-Soviet states.

In a statement, Bill Clinton said no one was better suited to advise him on Russian affairs than Talbott, noting that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton also relied on his counsel.

TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT?

"He was analytical, completely devoted to diplomacy, and on the level," Bill Clinton said. "With his expertise, we made real progress building trust between two former adversaries — moving beyond decades of confrontation to reduce the nuclear dangers future generations would inherit and build a Europe where more people could live in freedom and peace, including through the expansion of NATO and resolving ethnic conflicts in the Balkans. Together we laid the groundwork for greater cooperation while putting Russia on a path to democracy."

"Sadly, its current leader has taken the country in a different direction," Clinton added, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

He described Talbott as a "good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," and said, "Hillary and I will miss him very much."

After leaving government, Talbott served as president of the Brookings Institution from 2002 to 2017 and chaired the State Department’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board.

He is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren. His first wife, Brooke Shearer, died in 2009; he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Putin's grip on Crimea tested amid major blackout as Zelenskyy warns of looming Russian strike
item.description: A massive blackout crippled Crimea, testing Vladimir Putin's grip as outages hit Sevastopol and Simferopol and Zelenskyy warned of a new Russian strike.
item.content:encoded:
Russian President Vladimir Putin's control over Crimea faced renewed pressure Thursday as a massive blackout crippled the Russian-occupied peninsula, disrupting public transport and leaving people without heat, according to reports.

The blackout came after Ukrainian strikes had damaged the Kerch Strait Bridge last week, disrupting a key Russian military supply route, and as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Moscow was preparing another large-scale attack on Ukraine.

Russian-controlled utilities blamed the Crimea blackout on an accident at energy facilities outside the region, after reports of explosions and air raid sirens sounded across the Black Sea peninsula, according to the Kyiv Post.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence suggested that Russia was preparing to target the country's energy infrastructure, logistics networks and essential services.

"Unfortunately, the Russians are already completing preparations for a new massive strike," Zelenskyy wrote on X Thursday following a coordination meeting. "According to intelligence, energy facilities and logistics infrastructure, as well as essential services facilities in cities and communities, will once again be the targets."

The Ukrainian leader also urged residents to remain vigilant, warning of renewed missile attacks.

"In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats," Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address Thursday, according to Reuters. "And in Russia, they should know that we will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike."

In Crimea, Russian-controlled electricity provider Sevastopolenergo said that Sevastopol had lost power, while electricity restrictions affected Simferopol, Kerch, Alushta and Yevpatoria, according to Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda.

ZELENSKYY SAYS RUSSIA STRIKES HOMETOWN, CRITICIZES PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING

Streetcar services were also suspended in Yevpatoria and buses replaced trolleybuses on some routes in Simferopol. Parts of Kerch were also reportedly left without heating.

Russian-installed authorities had issued air raid alerts Thursday morning amid reports of explosions.

The blackout is the latest in a series of disruptions that have hit Crimea since late October, with Russian authorities blaming damage to power infrastructure.

The disruptions come amid mounting pressure on Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014 and has since used as a military and logistics hub for its operations against Ukraine.

The Kerch Strait Bridge, which connects the peninsula to mainland Russia, serves as a critical transportation link for Russian forces and has been targeted by Ukraine since Putin launched his invasion in 2022.

KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION

The bridge was built after the Russian annexation and opened in 2018, serving as a symbol of Moscow's control over the peninsula.

Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko also said seven people were wounded in an overnight Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital that damaged a shopping center and two other buildings, Reuters reported.

Zelenskyy also called for additional air defense assistance Thursday, emphasizing the need for interceptors for Patriot air defense systems and National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS).

"I expect a report from Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry on the results of its communication with our partners regarding the supply of air defenses — interceptors for Patriots and NASAMS are the key priority," Zelenskyy wrote.

It was the second time this week Zelenskyy had warned of preparations for another major Russian attack, according to Reuters.

item.title: Eagles erase 21-point deficit to stun Cowboys with biggest Thanksgiving comeback in NFL history
item.description: The Cowboys were up 31-10 and your Thanksgiving nap was looking like a fine idea until Joe Milton and the Eagles gave everyone on the couch a reason to get up.
item.content:encoded:
Look, if you saw the 3-7 Philadelphia Eagles visiting the 5-6 Dallas Cowboys and figured it was time for your Thanksgiving nap, I get it. The NFL stuck them between Bears-Lions and Chiefs-Bills. When Dallas went up 31-10 late in the third quarter, it looked like you’d timed it perfectly.

Hopefully, someone in your family had the decency to wake you up for the fourth quarter. The Eagles took their first lead Thursday with two seconds left, when Jake Elliott drilled the game-winner from the Cowboys’ star at midfield. Philly’s 39-38 win was the biggest comeback in NFL Thanksgiving history.

If you did sneak in a nap, the first half was the time to do it. By the time the Eagles and Cowboys kicked off, you’d already watched Caleb Williams hit Rome Odunze with three seconds left to give Chicago a 39-35 win. The Bears and Lions came in tied atop the NFC North, and Chicago left Detroit with a one-game lead.

CALEB WILLIAMS, WHO SEEMED TO DISRESPECT NATIONAL ANTHEM MONTHS AGO, SHOWS PATRIOTISM ON THANKSGIVING

Besides, you had to save some energy for Josh Allen vs. Patrick Mahomes on Thanksgiving night. The 9-1 Buffalo Bills were hosting the 8-2 Kansas City Chiefs in arguably the biggest game of the regular season so far.

Philly had already seen what this Cowboys offense could do. Dallas’ 38-21 win in Philadelphia last month kicked off a five-game stretch in which the Cowboys averaged 37.2 points per game. Two Dallas possessions into the rematch, they were already up 14-0.

Javonte Williams capped the 11-play, 77-yard opening drive with a 1-yard touchdown run. Then, on the ensuing Eagles possession, Quinnen Williams stuffed Saquon Barkley on fourth-and-1. Five plays later, KaVontae Turpin caught a short pass from Dak Prescott and sprinted up the sideline for a 31-yard score.

The Eagles finally got on the board with a 48-yard Jake Elliott field goal on their third drive, but Dallas answered right back. Prescott hit CeeDee Lamb for gains of 10 and 19 yards before Javonte Williams ran it in from the 12 for his second touchdown.

Eagles quarterback Joe Milton found DeVonta Smith on a 50-yard bomb to cut the deficit to 21-10 with 4:06 left in the first half. Dallas answered again, and the officials got plenty of screen time.

Three Eagles penalties gave the Cowboys 44 yards, including back-to-back pass interference calls that moved Dallas from the Philly 40 to the 1. After two Eagles stops, an offensive pass interference call on CeeDee Lamb wiped out a touchdown pass to Brevyn Spann-Ford and made it third-and-goal from the 12. Javonte Williams caught Prescott’s pass at the 8, dragged an Eagles defender to the goal line and fell across it for his third touchdown of the half.

By halftime, it looked a lot like Sunday against Tennessee. For the second time in five days, the Cowboys scored four first-half touchdowns and took an 18-point lead into the locker room. They led the Titans 27-9 and the Eagles 28-10.

For most of the third quarter, it looked like the second half would go the same way, too. Tennessee never got closer than 11 after halftime, and Brandon Aubrey drilled a 59-yard field goal to put Dallas up 31-10 with 3:35 left in the third. Then came two plays worth waking up for.

Milton found Smith for another bomb, this one a 45-yard touchdown with 15 seconds left in the quarter. Just 89 seconds of game time later, Ty Robinson blocked Bryan Anger’s punt, and Kenny Moore II scooped it up at the Dallas 3 and ran it in. Suddenly, it was 31-24 with nearly the entire fourth quarter left.

WHERE DOES AARON RODGERS’ INTERVIEW WITH PAT MCAFEE RANK AMONG THE WILDEST IN SPORTS HISTORY?

Prescott answered by hitting Lamb for 39 yards on second-and-16 and another 12 on third-and-8 before scrambling for a 14-yard touchdown himself. That put Dallas up 38-24 with 10:11 left. The two-touchdown cushion lasted all of 62 seconds.

Britain Covey returned the kickoff 55 yards, Milton found Smith twice, and then the Eagles quarterback ran one in himself from the 15. The Eagles went for two after cutting the deficit to eight, but Milton’s pass to Zach Ertz fell incomplete.

Philly forced a three-and-out, and Covey returned the punt 23 yards. With 7:37 left, the Eagles had the ball at the Dallas 49 with a chance to tie.

But DeMarvion Overshown sacked Milton on second down, and on third-and-15, Cobie Durant picked off a pass intended for Makai Lemon and returned it to the Eagles’ 48.

Dallas drove to the Philly 22, where Aubrey had a chance to make it a two-score game. Naturally, the guy who drilled one from 59 in the third quarter pulled this one wide left from 40. With 3:27 left, the Eagles still trailed 38-30 and had another shot to tie.

Milton took the Eagles 70 yards in four throws, the last a 24-yard touchdown to Makai Lemon with 2:10 left. He went right back to Lemon for the tie. This time the pass fell incomplete, and Dallas still led 38-36.

Because Philadelphia had all three timeouts and the two-minute warning, the Dallas offense needed two first downs to seal the victory. They got the first on a 15-yard strike from Prescott to Brevyn Spann-Ford on a second-and-8 play.

But they couldn't get the second. Javonte Williams had three straight carries to gain nine yards, leaving the Cowboys with a fourth-and-1 on the Eagles' 41-yard line and 55 seconds remaining. Instead of attempting a long field goal or punting, the Cowboys elected to go for a first down and the win.

Ty Robinson, who’d already blocked a punt, sacked Prescott on fourth-and-1. The Eagles got the ball back near midfield with 50 seconds left.

With seven seconds left and the ball at the Dallas 41, Philly sent Elliott out to win it.

He drilled it.

Hopefully everyone was awake to see it.

item.title: FLASHBACK: Two presidents pulled off secret Thanksgiving surprises for US troops — see the moments
item.description: Two Presidents pulled off secret Thanksgiving trips to war zones, with Donald Trump serving turkey at Bagram Airfield and George W. Bush visiting Iraq.
item.content:encoded:
Under a cloak of secrecy, two American presidents made surprise Thanksgiving visits to war zones, bringing a taste of home to U.S. troops serving thousands of miles from their families.

Sixteen years apart, President George W. Bush celebrated with American troops in Iraq in 2003, while President Donald Trump served Thanksgiving dinner to service members in Afghanistan in 2019. Both visits were carried out under tight secrecy, catching troops by surprise as they spent the holiday far from home.

Trump secretly traveled to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, where he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war.

INSIDE TRUMP’S INTIMATE MEETING WITH NATION’S BRAVEST SOLDIERS DURING WHIRLWIND TEXAS TRIP

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best, and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time, later adding, "And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you."

The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.

ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE'

During the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He said his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict.

Less than two years later, President Joe Biden oversaw the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021.

WOUNDED MARINES RELIVE THE HARROWING KABUL AIRPORT ATTACK IN EXPLOSIVE NEW FOX NATION DOCUMENTARY

The withdrawal unfolded as the Taliban rapidly seized control of Afghanistan, culminating in the fall of Kabul and a frantic evacuation at the city's airport.

Sixteen years earlier, Bush pulled off a similar Thanksgiving surprise in Iraq , secretly flying into Baghdad International Airport on Nov. 27, 2003, to celebrate with American troops just eight months after launching the U.S.-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein's regime.

GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS

Bush stunned hundreds of service members when he appeared at their Thanksgiving dinner, emerging to cheers and applause before helping serve a traditional holiday meal and posing for photos with troops stationed far from home.

"I can't think of a finer group of folks to have Thanksgiving dinner with than you all," Bush told the troops at the time.

"We're proud of you," he added. "Today, Americans are gathering with their loved ones to give thanks for the many blessings in our lives."

News of his trip was not even released until Air Force One had already left Iraq.

US FACES ANOTHER MAJOR MIDDLE EAST TROOP WITHDRAWAL, BUT THREAT REMAINS

Bush's visit came as American forces battled a growing insurgency following the fall of Saddam Hussein's government earlier that year. Despite Bush's declaration in May that major combat operations had ended, U.S. troops continued to face deadly attacks as the military worked to stabilize the country.

Just weeks later, U.S. forces captured Saddam Hussein in December 2003.

item.title: TPUSA mourns Florida high school chapter president killed with family in devastating plane crash
item.description: Turning Point USA's student program is mourning Hunter Stokes, 16, who led its Fort Myers chapter, after the Cessna 210 he rode in crashed off Horn Island, Mississippi.
item.content:encoded:
Turning Point USA's student program mourned the death of a Florida high school chapter president this week after the teen and five members of his family died Tuesday in a plane crash off the Mississippi coast.

The organization said it was "heartbroken" over the loss of Hunter Stokes, 16, who led the Fort Myers High School Club America chapter.

"Hunter was a young patriot who loved his country and led by example," TPUSA Students said in a Wednesday post on X.

SIX FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN PLANE CRASH ON WAY HOME FROM FISHING TRIP IDENTIFIED

"From attending our Chapter Leadership Summit this summer to helping lead his chapter’s 9/11 Flag Run in honor of the victims of the September 11 attacks, Hunter was dedicated to making a difference in his community," the statement continued. "We are grateful to have had Hunter as part of our TPUSA family. Please join us in lifting his family, friends, and fellow chapter members up in prayer."

Hunter was killed in the crash alongside his father, Brent Stokes, 50; his aunt and uncle, Arlyn and Michael Knox, both 43; and his cousins, Charles Holden Knox, 12, and Truett Knox, 10, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr.

DOZENS MISSING AFTER PASSENGER FERRY SINKS AS RESCUERS SCOUR SOUTH PACIFIC COASTLINE

GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS

The group was returning to Florida after a family fishing trip.

"They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family," both families said in a joint statement to The News-Press.

The six were aboard a Cessna 210 piloted by Brent Stokes when the aircraft went down two miles off Horn Island, Mississippi, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Officials said the plane entered a descent of 10,000 feet per minute prior to the crash.

GOT A TIP?

Air traffic controllers advised Stokes of precipitation and adverse weather shortly before losing contact with the aircraft at about 3:45 p.m. local time, the New York Post and the FAA reported.

Brent Stokes was the president and CEO of Stokes Marine Inc., while Arlyn and Michael Knox led Knox Technologies, an IT company based in Fort Myers.

St. Cecilia Catholic Community on Wednesday said Brent and Hunter Stokes were former parishioners.

"Please keep the Stokes and Knox families in your prayers during this time of loss," the community wrote in a Facebook post. "May the Lord grant eternal rest and the promise of the Resurrection. Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Olympic trailblazer Anita DeFrantz, longtime advocate for women in sports, dies at 74
item.description: Anita DeFrantz, the first Black American woman on the IOC and a 1976 rowing bronze medalist, died at 74, leaving a legacy of fighting for women in sport.
item.content:encoded:
The sports world is mourning the loss of an Olympic trailblazer.

Anita DeFrantz has died, the International Olympic Committee and U.S. Olympic Committe said. She was 74. No cause of death was not immediately disclosed, although DeFrantz was believed to have been in declining health in recent years.

DeFrantz won a bronze medal in rowing at the 1976 Olympics, later becoming a powerful advocate for women in the male-dominated world of Olympic policymaking. She broke barriers throughout her career, becoming the first American woman and first Black American appointed to the IOC in 1986 before becoming the first woman to serve as an IOC vice president in 1997.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

DeFrantzalso was vice president of the organizing committee for the LA Olympics in 1984 and served as chair of the IOC’s Women in Sport Commission for two decades.

IOC President Kirsty Coventry, an Olympic swimmer who has credited DeFrantz with helping her rise to the highest position in the Olympic movement, described DeFrantz as "a mentor, a friend and a true inspiration to me, and to so many others around the world."

FIFA AWARDS 2031 WOMEN'S WORLD CUP TO THE UNITED STATES WITH MAJOR REVENUE EXPECTATIONS LEADING THE WAY

"From my earliest days in the Olympic Movement, she showed me what courageous leadership looked like, and what was possible for women in sport," Coventry said.

Edwin Moses, the record-setting hurdler and a contemporary of DeFrantz, said, "every woman who has a high-level position in sports today, they can thank Anita DeFrantz."

DeFrantz won bronze in the 1976 Olympics as captain of the women’s eight team in Montreal. She trained for an Olympic return and, in 1980, gained a sense of the disconnect between athletes and the boardrooms that made decisions on their behalf.

DeFrantz was part of the U.S. team that never made the trip to the boycotted 1980 Moscow Olympics. As spokeswoman for the U.S. athletes’ advisory council, she later led a lawsuit against the U.S. Olympic Committee, which had authorized the boycott under pressure from the Carter administration.

That experience marked the beginning of her effort to earn a seat at the table where those decisions were made.

Before her induction into the Team USA Hall of Fame, DeFrantz recalled realizing how much work remained when she attended her first IOC meeting in 1986.

JAPANESE BOWLING PIONEER RITSUKO NAKAYAMA, FIRST WOMAN TO BOWL PROFESSIONAL PERFECT GAME, DIES AT 84

"I walked in and I thought, ‘This is odd,’" she told The Associated Press in 2025. "It was this cavernous room" and of the 90 or so committee members, she was one of only five women.

"We had to help people open their minds a little," she said.

Women made up half of the 10,500 athletes at the 2024 Paris Games. Today, 46 of the IOC’s 106 members are women.

U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee CEO Sarah Hirshland and chairman Gene Sykes remember DeFrantz as "one of the most consequential Olympians our nation has ever known."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Unforgiving rim denies Arkansas a miracle comeback against Michigan State on Thanksgiving
item.description: No. 11 Michigan State escaped with a 70-67 Thanksgiving win after Jordan Smith Jr.’s potential tying three rattled out in the final seconds.
item.content:encoded:
With 1:18 left in a game played on Thanksgiving, Arkansas trailed No. 11 Michigan State by 10 and the Spartans were at the free-throw line. If you’d offered John Calipari one shot to send the game to overtime, I’m guessing he’d have taken it before you finished the question.

Well, he got his shot. Jordan Smith Jr. pulled up from 29 feet, and the ball found just about every part of the rim at Little Caesars Arena before it finally bounced out. Michigan State escaped Detroit with a 70-67 win to move to 6-1, and Arkansas fell to 4-3.

Arkansas took a 31-27 lead into halftime, pushed it to eight early in the second half and still led 47-40 with 13:31 left. If you’re a Michigan State fan who watched the Spartans lose at Tennessee nine days earlier, I can’t blame you for thinking, "Uh-oh." They’d made all of three baskets in the second half in Knoxville and shot 18% for the game.

MICHIGAN STATE'S PUTRID SHOOTING PERFORMANCE IN LOSS TO TENNESSEE PRODUCES LAUGHABLE FINAL BOX SCORE

Down seven in Detroit, Jeremy Fears Jr. hit a three. Then he found Jesse McCulloch for a hook shot and Coen Carr for the dunk that tied it.

Michigan State scored 15 straight, and by the time Kur Teng buried his third three in less than two minutes, the Spartans led 64-51 with 4:55 left. That’s a 24-4 run. The same team that went 3-for-26 after halftime at Tennessee went 17-for-21 (81%) in the second half against Arkansas.

Michigan State still led 68-58 when Fears stepped to the line with 1:18 left. He missed the front end of a one-and-one, but Arkansas still needed 10 points just to pull even.

COLLEGE BASKETBALL GETS A NEW NO. 1 AS THREE TEAMS FALL OUT OF THE AP TOP FIVE IN A SINGLE WEEK

So how did the Razorbacks make it interesting in the final seconds? For starters, Michigan State just couldn’t grab a defensive rebound. The Razorbacks missed two threes on the same possession before Billy Richmond III tipped the ball in with 1:03 to go.

Then Smith picked off a Fears pass. On the ensuing possession, Arkansas rebounded a missed free throw AND a missed three before Smith found Richmond for the three that cut it to 68-64.

Jeremy Fears Jr. made both free throws with 16 seconds left to put Michigan State back up six. Then came the call I’d still be asking about if I were Tom Izzo.

Smith drove to the basket and spun past Fears for a layup. The officials called Fears for a foul, counted the basket and gave Smith a chance to cut it to three with 10 seconds left.

Did Fears foul Smith? Absolutely. Smith still had his back to the basket and was about 13 feet from the hoop when the contact came. Smith finished his spin, took another full step and then laid the ball in. How much continuation are we giving this guy? Even the CBS crew thought the foul should have been ruled on the floor.

Smith made the free throw with 10 seconds left, Fears missed the front end of a one-and-one with eight seconds left, and guess who came down with the rebound? Smith had six seconds and the length of the floor to find a three. From 29 feet, he came about as close as you can get.

If you laid 5.5 with Michigan State, how good did you feel with 1:18 left? Your team was up 10, and you had a career 81% free-throw shooter at the line. You could give up a couple of garbage-time buckets and still cash.

Fears missed the front end, Arkansas grabbed four offensive rebounds in two possessions, and Michigan State threw the ball away in between. And after all that? You were still covering when Fears hit both free throws to make it 70-64 with 16 seconds left.

It took that generous continuation call to put Arkansas back inside the number. Then your 81% free-throw shooter went back to the line with eight seconds left and missed the front end of another one-and-one.

That left Michigan State bettors rooting for the same guy who’d just cost them the cover. If Smith’s three drops, you get five more minutes to win by six. If you had Arkansas +5.5, on the other hand, you had every reason to cheer when that ball finally bounced out.

Which probably raised a fair question from across the Thanksgiving table: "Wait, didn’t you bet on Arkansas?"

item.title: Democrats, Republicans find rare common ground when asked what they're thankful for
item.description: Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill may clash on policy, but this Thanksgiving, lawmakers say family is what they're most thankful for.
item.content:encoded:
An ocean of ideological differences separates Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill, but they're largely in agreement over one thing this Thanksgiving, and it's usually miles away from Washington, D.C.

"I'm thankful for family," Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo., told Fox News Digital. "It's what drives me to keep going, to keep doing this, keep fighting for the country."

Families across America are gathering for Thanksgiving, kicking off a holiday season that's meant for reflection and refocusing on things that matter most. And members of Congress who spoke with Fox News Digital about that special day are no different.

"You know, elections can be a bumpy road in many ways, and it's easy to take a shot at somebody who's running — we put ourselves out there. But it's the family, really, and I'm grateful that my wife and my three kids who are in their 20s are so supportive," Rep. John Mannion, D-N.Y., said. "So that's what I'm thankful for."

Reps. Randy Fine, R-Fla., and Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., singled out their children.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

"I'm very grateful to how great my boys are doing despite the challenges of this job, and just my whole family for putting up with all of this and being there for me," Fine said.

Burchett told Fox News Digital he was "more than blessed."

"I've got a beautiful wife and a daughter, and I never thought I was gonna have a family. And I prayed, asked Jesus that I'd have a family, and I got one, dadgum it, and it is wonderful," Burchett said.

Rep. Mike Quigley, D-Ill., said he was grateful for the U.S.'s ability to still come together despite people's many differences.

SOUND OFF: WILL DEMOCRATS AND REPUBLICANS COME TOGETHER FOR THE GOOD OF THE COUNTRY?

"I'm most thankful that this country still reminds itself that there's more that unites us than divides us," Quigley said.

Two more Democrats said they were thankful for their party’s success in the midterm elections.

"I'm thankful for the excitement of next year, to get things done," said Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill.

Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., said he was thankful for "an opportunity to make a difference in people's lives."

"Democrats got a huge majority, and that allows us to help people," Thanedar, who lost his own re-election bid, said.

item.title: Georgia man accused of killing wife after dispute over children's Christmas presents
item.description: A Georgia man was charged with murder after police say he fatally shot his wife following an argument over Christmas presents for their four children.
item.content:encoded:
A Georgia man was arrested after allegedly shooting and killing his wife following an argument about Christmas presents they purchased for their four children.

Gene McCall Allen, 33, was arrested Friday and charged with the murder of his wife of about eight years, Bonnie Lashea Allen, 32, according to the Walker County Sheriff's Office. He is being held at the Walker County Jail without bond.

Deputies responded to the couple's home in Rossville, south of Chattanooga, Tennessee, on the evening of Nov. 14 following a report of a woman who had been shot, according to an incident report obtained by PEOPLE. Deputies found Gene Allen performing CPR on his wife, who had been shot in the head.

A deputy also found a gun resting on a closet shelf facing toward the room, according to the report.

MARATHONER ASKED HUSBAND ABOUT ‘POWDERY’ WATER BEFORE FATAL FALL – THEN POLICE FOUND HIS GOOGLE SEARCHES

Gene Allen told deputies that the gun was inside the closet when it went off, PEOPLE reported. He also allegedly told authorities he and his wife argued earlier that day about the Christmas presents they bought for their children, saying she raised concerns about the cost of shipping and the quality of the gifts.

The report also notes Gene Allen said he had four beers that day.

Bonnie Allen's family created a GoFundMe to help the children with their everyday needs, including clothing, according to the fundraising site. Her children are now being cared for by family members.

"Bonnie LaShae’s children & family [are] heartbroken over the tragic loss of a mother, daughter, sister, aunt and loved one who was taken far too soon. In the blink of an eye, her little children have lost their mother, and their lives have been changed forever," the fundraiser states.

"No family should ever have to experience this kind of heartbreak, especially these little ones who have so much life ahead of them," it added.

The GoFundMe has raised about $12,000 as of Thursday evening.

In her obituary, Bonnie was remembered as "an amazing mother who never missed an opportunity to support her children."

FLORIDA DEPUTY KILLED EX-GIRLFRIEND OVER A TV, THEN HIMSELF, SHERIFF SAYS

"Whether cheering them on at a ball game or encouraging other children, she was always there, proudly showing her love and support. She was her children’s biggest fan, greatest encourager, and strongest supporter," the obituary reads.

"She was a blessing to everyone fortunate enough to know her. Bonnie had a joy that was contagious and a personality that could light up any room. She was fun-loving, full of life, and always brought happiness wherever she went. A strong, natural leader, Bonnie had a way of encouraging others, making people feel welcome, and leaving a lasting impression on everyone she met. She will be remembered for her beautiful spirit, unwavering love for her family, her faith, and the joy she brought into so many lives," it added.

item.title: Caleb Williams' heroics have Bears thinking No. 1 seed in NFC playoffs
item.description: Caleb Williams hit Rome Odunze for a go-ahead TD with 3 seconds left as the Chicago Bears rallied past the Detroit Lions to grab first in the NFC North.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears opened Thanksgiving with a statement win that strengthened their path to the NFC’s No. 1 seed.

Caleb Williams engineered a late fourth-quarter rally from an 11-point deficit before delivering a highlight-reel touchdown pass to the back corner of the end zone, where only Rome Odunze could make the catch. The score gave the Bears their first lead of the game.

The 39-35 win also gave the Bears the advantage in the hard-fought NFC North division.

"Rome is not even the primary on that one," Chicago coach Ben Johnson said. "Caleb did a good job, just working through it, and the guys gave him a clean pocket."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Bears have now won six straight, while the Lions’ six-game winning streak came to an end after they failed to make a defensive stop late.

"We needed this one," Johnson added. "They knew that. They weathered the storm."

Williams finished the day with 345 yards with two touchdown passes after trailing by 11 points midway through the fourth quarter following Jahmyr Gibbs’ 70-yard run for his third score of the game.

AMON-RA ST BROWN KICKS OFF THANKSGIVING WITH RIDICULOUS ONE-HANDED GRAB, STANKY LEG CELEBRATION

Chicago became just the third team to rally from a deficit of 11 points or more in the fourth quarter to win on Thanksgiving , joining the 1980 Bears who did it against Detroit and the 1962 New York Titans who came back to beat the Denver Broncos on the holiday.

AARON RODGERS VS MIKE MCCARTHY: TIMELINE OF BELOVED SUPER BOWL DUO'S DESCENT INTO BAFFLING NFL SOAP OPERA

The Bears had the ball earlier in the fourth with a chance to at least tie the game after Jared Goff’s pass went through Jameson Williams’ hands and was picked off by Dillon Thieneman at the Chicago 21 and returned 18 yards.

Chicago turned it over on downs on the ensuing possession, going for it on fourth-and-3 from the Detroit 42.

The Green Bay Packers, who entered the game in last place in the NFC North, lost to the Los Angeles Rams in the NFL’s first Thanksgiving Eve game. The Minnesota Vikings, who sit in third place, will face Kirk Cousins’ former team, the Atlanta Falcons, on Sunday.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Iran accuses Zelenskyy of 'false flag' Kuwait drone strike op to get Trump's attention
item.description: A former Iran nuclear adviser claimed Thursday the Kuwait drone attack was a Ukrainian "false flag" staged to get President Donald Trump's attention.
item.content:encoded:
A former adviser to Iran's nuclear negotiating team accused Ukraine on Thursday of orchestrating a deadly drone attack in Kuwait to prove its worth to President Donald Trump, as Tehran continued to deny responsibility.

And while Kuwaiti and Italian officials blamed Iran for the strike, which killed two Italian defense technicians and wounded two others, Iran’s embassy in Rome warned against "false flag" operations it said were aimed at widening the Persian Gulf conflict and now drawing Europe into the crisis.

Mohammad Marandi, who served as an adviser during talks with the U.S. in Pakistan and has been dubbed Iran's "English-language mouthpiece," claimed Ukrainian forces were operating across the Middle East, including in northern Iraq and Syria, also in remarks reported by the Fars News Agency, which is affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

IRAN TARGETS US AIR BASE IN KUWAIT AFTER US DEFENSIVE STRIKES AMID CRITICISM FROM GULF STATES

"It is widely believed in Iran that the attack on Kuwait was a false flag operation, likely carried out by the Ukrainian regime, because its operatives are now present across the region, including in northern Iraq and Syria. Ukraine aims to demonstrate its potential to Trump," Marandi said on X.

Fars also cited a security source who claimed Ukrainian operatives had deployed thousands of drones and other unmanned aircraft in several Middle Eastern countries, including Iraq's Kurdistan region, according to Iran International.

Kuwait's Defense Ministry said falling debris from the interception of Iranian drones struck a military facility Thursday, initially wounding four people. Two Italian nationals later died of their injuries.

A Kuwaiti national and a Pakistani national were also wounded and taken to a hospital for treatment. The ministry did not disclose the facility's precise location.

Italy's Foreign Ministry confirmed that the two Italian nationals were employees of Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian subsidiary of German defense manufacturer Rheinmetall.

"An explosion caused by a drone attack ... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working," the ministry said in a statement.

The victims were identified as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, of Formia, Italy, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, of Rome, Italian news agency ANSA reported.

EUROPE ASSASSINATION SCHEME EMERGES AS IRAN DENIES DC 'DIRTY BOMB' PLOT AMID TRUMP WARNING

The men had been performing maintenance on detection antennas for the Skyguard air defense system.

Iran's embassy in Rome rejected allegations that Tehran was responsible for the attack, warning of alleged efforts to draw European countries into the Middle East conflict.

"The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran also draws the international community's attention to 'false flag' activities and operations aimed at expanding the scope of the conflict, linking disputes in other regions to the Persian Gulf crisis, drawing Europe into the crisis, and exacerbating the current critical situation, and calls on everyone to remain vigilant in this regard."

Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had spoken with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and offered to cooperate in an investigation into the deadly incident.

"In calls with my Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts, expressed condolences over deaths of Italian citizens in Kuwait," Araghchi wrote. "The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war.

"We stand ready to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the incident," he added.

TOP GULF OFFICIAL OFFERS GLIMMER OF HOPE ON TRUMP-IRAN NUCLEAR TALKS AS THREAT OF WAR HANGS OVER REGION

Kuwait, a key U.S. ally in the Persian Gulf, has repeatedly come under Iranian attack since the U.S. and Israel launched military operations against Iran on Feb. 28.

Ukraine has deployed drone specialists and interceptor drones to the Middle East to help defend against Iranian attacks, expanding its regional defense cooperation by sharing technology and military expertise developed during its war with Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in March that Kyiv had sent interceptor drones and specialists to help protect U.S. military installations in Jordan at Washington's request.

Ukraine also announced that teams of military specialists had been deployed to Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia to help defend against Iranian drone attacks.

"Ukraine has the greatest experience in the world in countering attack drones," Zelenskyy said in March, adding that "without our experience, it will be very difficult for the Gulf region, the entire Middle East, and partners in Europe and America to build strong protection."

item.title: Trademark Dan Campbell fourth-down gamble backfires, opening door to stunning Bears comeback victory
item.description: Caleb Williams hit Rome Odunze for a six-yard touchdown with three seconds left as the Chicago Bears stole first place in the NFC North from Detroit.
item.content:encoded:
The legend of Dan Campbell took a hit this Thanksgiving Day. A new legend might be growing around Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson.

When Chicago Bears coaches and players met on Thanksgiving eve to discuss Thursday's game against the Detroit Lions, Johnson drove the conversation toward taking stuff from the Lions.

The Lions were the division leaders.

They've been the NFC North's most consistently successful team for years.

CALEB WILLIAMS, WHO ONCE SEEMED TO DISRESPECT NATIONAL ANTHEM, SHOWED PATRIOTISM ON THANKSGIVING

"They were at the top of the division," Johnson said. "They had what we wanted."

And the Bears went and got it. Now they are the NFC North's leaders and de facto best team in one of the league's best divisions.

But not before it was all delivered in electric fashion.

Caleb Williams connected with wide receiver Rome Odunze, who was not the primary receiver on the play, in the back corner of the end zone for a six-yard touchdown with three seconds to play to give the Bears the winning score.

"Absolutely incredible," CBS play-by-play voice Jim Nantz said, describing the moment.

And it was that because the TD gave the Bears their first lead of the game after the Lions led for 59:57.

It gave Williams – who had a viral moment during the national anthem – his first career victory over the Bears. The Lions swept the Bears the first two years the third-year Chicago quarterback has been in the league.

"This shows how far we've come in the last year-and-a-half," Johnson said. "Proud of the offense the way they handled that last drive."

NICK FOLES BELIEVES BEARS ARE TEAM TO BEAT IN LOADED NFC NORTH: 'SOMETHING'S BREWING IN CHICAGO'

This result meant the Lions wasted a Herculean performance by Jahmyr Gibbs. He rushed for 205 yards. He averaged 9.8 yards per carry. He scored three touchdowns.

And it wasn't enough.

"They did what they had to do to win that game," Campbell said.

Stunning stuff.

As the Bears walked off the field to a Turducken celebration in honor of John Madden – a tribute the NFL set for all three Thursday games – Campbell had to be beating himself up.

Chicago's game winning score, you see, came after the Lions' coach passed on a 51-yard field goal attempt by his long-range kicker Jake Bates.

With 2:22 to play, Campbell gambled on closing out the game by going for it on fourth-and-4 from the Bears' 33 yard line. Quarterback Jared Goff completed his attempt to Gibbs but the running back was stopped after only a one-yard gain.

This was a deeply controversial decision, although not to Campbell.

"I thought we'd get it, I mean, first of all," Campbell said. "I really believed we were going to get that."

Bates has been something a long-range assassin for the Lions in his time as their kicker. He has connected on 12 of 20 field goals of 50 yards or more.

He has converted seven field goals of 56 yards or more.

He has four career field goals of 58 yards.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Letting him try that long field goal was not easy to dismiss.

"I don't regret that," Campbell said. "I wish we'd have made that but sometimes that happens, you know?"

Yes, we know. We saw.

item.title: Universities, schools nationwide use Thanksgiving as chance to promote 'Day of Mourning' and decolonization
item.description: Campus Thanksgiving events have been reframed as a "National Day of Mourning" for Indigenous remembrance, with Salem State and Pratt citing historical harm.
item.content:encoded:
Thanksgiving is a day of celebration and spending time with family for the vast majority of Americans, but for several students on college campuses across the country, the national holiday is a source of anguish that is being expressed in the form of protests and counter-programming events.

On Nov. 18, George Washington University hosted an event called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration" that was described as a chance for students to examine Thanksgiving, Christmas and Independence Day through an intersectional lens, including experiences of "belonging, exclusion, cultural erasure, and historical harm."

"Through facilitated dialogue and shared reflection, students will engage in meaningful conversations about historical memory, social responsibility, and the complexities of celebrating within a diverse society," the student life event description read.

At the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee, the American Indian Student Center & Electa Quinney Institute for American Indian Education hosted a Nov. 17 event called "AlterNative Giving," which was described as "a community gathering that offers a meaningful alternative to the traditional Thanksgiving narrative. Instead of focusing on colonial histories, we come together to honor Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and giving."

TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN ‘MISSES CORE IDEOLOGY' AND MUST TARGET LINGERING DANGER ON CAMPUSES, WATCHDOG WARNS

Salem State University promoted an event that labeled Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" and told students the land they are being educated on was stolen from Indigenous people.

"The land occupied by Salem State University is part of the traditional and ancestral homeland of the Massachusett tribe," the school’s website posted. "We acknowledge the genocide and forced removal of the Massachusett tribe and their kin from their summer home in Nâmkek."

CALIFORNIA COLLEGE LECTURER REMOVED AFTER ERUPTING AT STUDENT OVER QUESTION ON NATIVE AMERICANS

A review of university calendars found several examples lamenting the downsides of Thanksgiving, including Occidental College, which said the holiday is a "reminder of settler colonialism and its devastating impact on Indigenous individuals, communities and tribes."

The Pratt Institute lists "National Day of Mourning" as an occasion for Indigenous remembrance and reflection, and the University at Albany lists the holiday as "National Day of Mourning/Thanksgiving."

The colonial messaging around Thanksgiving isn't limited to universities but is also occurring at elementary and high schools, including in Loudoun County, Virginia, where a parent recently pushed back in an interview with Fox News about school lesson plans teaching children that Thanksgiving is a "Day of Mourning."

On its website, the San Diego County Office of Education explained that "November is Native American Heritage Month, a time to honor the diversity, history, and living cultures of Native peoples. It is also the month when Thanksgiving is observed in the United States, a holiday that carries very different meanings for different people, including many Native communities."

Oregon’s Bethel School District links to a "Decolonizing Thanksgiving: A Toolkit for Combatting Racism in Schools" on its official Equity, Access & Inclusion webpage. Listed under teaching resources, the toolkit appears alongside material about honoring Native peoples on Thanksgiving.

item.title: Chris Van Hollen gains celebrity donor backing as Fonda, De Niro and others support ditching Schumer in letter
item.description: Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro and other celebrities and Democratic donors said they supported Sen. Chris Van Hollen over Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.
item.content:encoded:
A group of about 35 Hollywood stars and Democratic donors signed a letter Tuesday supporting Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., over Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate Majority Leader.

"The Senate Democratic leader will be chosen behind closed doors, by secret ballot," the letter said, according to The New York Times. "No senator will ever have to tell voters, or us, how they voted. We believe a decision this consequential deserves public accountability."

Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro, Chelsea Handler, Marisa Tomei, Padma Lakshmi and David Mandel are among the signatories of the letter, the Times reported.

SCHUMER'S FORMER ALLY MOUNTS LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE AS DEMOCRATS FACE RARE INTERNAL POWER STRUGGLE

Morris Pearl, a former BlackRock executive, and V, born Eve Ensler, the author of "The Vagina Monologues," also signed the letter, according to the Times. Both had donated to Schumer in the past.

They say they donated or helped to raise about $23 million for Democratic candidates in House and Senate races this election cycle. Van Hollen announced he would challenge Schumer earlier this month.

The donors and celebrities argue that re-electing Schumer was not what the Democratic electorate wanted, according to the Times.

"This is an opportunity. This is a window," Handler said, according to the Times. "We need to, like, get the ball and run with it. And I don’t believe that Chuck Schumer is going to do that."

MARK RUFFALO DOUBLES DOWN ON CALL TO OUST SCHUMER OVER 'ENTRENCHED RELIGIOUS BELIEFS AND LOYALTIES'

Schumer's office did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The group of donors expressed frustration over Schumer's constrained support for progressive candidates in the midterm elections, the Times reported.

"Americans voted for the change necessary to fight the corruption, cruelty and policies of Trump and his Epstein-class cronies," De Niro said in a statement to the Times. "That’s why I’m supporting change in Senate leadership."

De Niro also called Van Hollen a "fierce fighter."

SCHUMER FACES MUTINY FROM NEWLY ELECTED SENATE DEMS AS PARTY PREPARES TO SEIZE POWER

The race for majority leader will be contested for the first time in three decades, and both Schumer and Van Hollen believe they have or can get the 28 votes needed to claim the mantle of Democratic leader and become majority leader.

Neither senator has publicly locked down enough support to eclipse the magic number.

BERNIE SANDERS SAYS HE WON'T BACK SCHUMER AS PUSH FOR NEW LEADERSHIP GAINS STEAM

Van Hollen has the support of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., Peggy Flanagan, D-Minn., and Troy Jackson, D-Maine, as well as Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., and Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore.

Slotkin announced last week she would be backing Van Hollen.

"I've been clear as well that I don't think that Sen. Schumer is best positioned to be our next leader. I'm encouraged that people like Chris Van Hollen got in the race, and because I've been clear that I wasn't supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen," Slotkin stated in a video posted to social media.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"But I think no matter the outcome, it's going to be imperative for our leaders to demonstrate how they're going to incorporate that next generation, and what big and bold ideas, specifically, they're going to put forward in the first 100 days," she said.

Van Hollen shared Slotkin's post on X and wrote, "@SenatorSlotkin & I agree: the American people spoke, and we need new leadership in the United States Senate. Now is the time to act boldly, and we’re going to work together to deliver results."

item.title: MAC admits that officials incorrectly cost Kent State touchdown with blown call against Eastern Michigan
item.description: The Mid-American Conference admitted officials erred overturning Kent State's touchdown against Eastern Michigan, citing insufficient video evidence.
item.content:encoded:
Officiating in college football has become a major, major problem.

Earlier this season, the Michigan Wolverines miraculously escaped against Western Michigan thanks to a controversial second being added to the game clock due to incorrect replay review procedures. While the MAC initially accepted the results, they then issued a statement criticizing how the situation was handled.

The Big 12 Conference admitted to several officiating mistakes, most of which benefited the BYU Cougars. During their game against Notre Dame, the referees failed to notice that the Irish should have had one second left to try and pull off a comeback win.

CLOCK CONTROVERSY: NCAA SAYS OFFICIALS BOTCHED REPLAY PROTOCOL IN MICHIGAN'S WIN OVER WESTERN MICHIGAN

"Following the Big 12's review of the final play of Saturday's Notre Dame-BYU game, it was determined that time remained on the clock when the ball hit the ground and the play was incorrectly cleared by the replay officiating crew," they explained in a statement. "The Conference will conduct a complete review of its end-of-game officiating process in advance of next week's games."

Then there was the inexplicable handling of the end of the BYU-UCF game, where a facemask penalty flag was picked up, and the Knights were incorrectly assessed a 10-second runoff at the end of regulation. Amazingly, the next week, the Cougars were given a touchdown on a fumble recovery that should not have been allowed thanks to a blown whistle.

In the SEC, the Texas-Missouri game featured several contentious calls that went the Longhorns' way, including the most absurd, awarding Arch Manning and Texas a first down on a fumble, though his arm was clearly moving forward. Analysts were so critical of the officiating in that game that they drew a rebuke from Greg Sankey afterward.

Notre Dame-Miami came down to what looked to be a massive touchdown catch for the Irish, waved off as incomplete. Those are just a few examples. And now we have another one. This time, ironically, involving MAC officials.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

During some recent late-night MACtion, a Kent State appeared to come down with a walk-off touchdown catch to beat Eastern Michigan. After an insane five-minute review process, the officials overturned it, based on, well, not much, and handed the win to the Eagles.

THE ABSOLUTE WORST CALL OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON HAPPENED LAST NIGHT WHILE YOU WERE SLEEPING

On Wednesday, the conference admitted that the officials erred in making the call and that Kent State should have won the game.

In a statement, they acknowledged that there was "insufficient video evidence to overturn the ruling on the field."

"The video evidence did not meet the clear and obvious standard required to overturn the ruling on the field," they added. "The decision to overturn the touchdown was incorrect, and the original ruling should have been upheld. The Mid-American Conference recognizes the significance of this error and regrets its impact on the outcome of the game. Our student-athletes, coaches, institutions and fans deserve the highest standards of officiating. The Conference remains committed to those standards and to maintaining the competitive integrity of our contests."

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Kent State head coach Mark Carney told ESPN that he was "heartbroken" by the outcome.

"In 25-plus years of playing and coaching college football, I have never felt the disappointment I felt last night postgame," Carney said. "Heartbroken for our players and staff who pour so much of themselves into what we do - especially those playing their last game of college football. We are extremely proud of the way our young men represent Kent State, our football program, and themselves."

Man, it doesn't get worse than that. Having the outcome of a game be directly affected by the officials making the wrong ruling. You have to feel terrible for Kent State players, fans, and coaches. And frustrating that officiating continues to be such a disaster when there's no excuse for it to be. Gotta be better and let the MACtion dictate the outcome, not the refs.

item.title: ‘Charlie Brown’ voice actor received zero residuals for nearly 50 years due to banned ’70s contract
item.description: Todd Barbee, the voice of Charlie Brown in "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving," says he got no residuals for decades until SAG-AFTRA renegotiated old contracts.
item.content:encoded:
Good grief — it turns out the voice of Charlie Brown didn't even make peanuts in residuals.

Todd Barbee was just 10 when his father's connection to producer Lee Mendelson landed him the iconic role of Charlie Brown in 1973's "A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving." Generations grew up watching his performance on network TV, yet Barbee, now 63, revealed to host Joseph Sibilia on his podcast, "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia," that he didn’t receive residual checks until about six years ago.

"Aside from the bountiful residuals I'm sure you've collected for the last 50-plus years, what has been the most rewarding part of being a part of the 'Peanuts' legacy?" Sibilia asked Barbee.

‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS

"Well, let me correct you on one front," Barbee replied. "We were actually under an old contractual relationship from the '70s that is no longer allowed by Screen Actors Guild and AFTRA, which is American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. The contract was a buyout, and that is not allowed by the unions anymore. I think it was overturned in the '80s."

"So, we did not receive any residuals at all," Barbee noted. "In fact, I didn't receive a single residual until about six years ago."

The initial gig paid "pretty handsomely" at the time "in 1970 dollars." He used his paycheck to help his mother buy the house that she still lives in to this day after his parents divorced. However, he didn't see any residual checks, no matter how massive the special became as a holiday tradition.

WATCH: CHARLIE BROWN VOICE ACTOR TODD BARBEE WENT DECADES WITHOUT ‘PEANUTS’ RESIDUALS

"Peanuts" made its debut on Oct. 2, 1950. The travails of the "little round-headed kid" Charlie Brown and his pals eventually ran in more than 2,600 newspapers, reaching millions of readers in 75 countries.

According to Barbee, everything changed after union renegotiations around streaming rights following Apple TV's acquisition of the "Peanuts" catalog. The streaming service obtained the exclusive rights to the "Peanuts" catalog in 2020, including the widely beloved "A Charlie Brown Christmas."

"During the big strike, writers' strike and everything that happened about five or six years ago ... Screen Actors Guild renegotiated some of these things," said Barbee. "And they determined Apple TV right now actually has the entire 'Peanuts' catalog. And what Screen Actors did [was say], 'Look, that doesn't have anything to do with these old contracts. That was for broadcast television. You're a streaming service. And as such, you need to pay these people current residuals.'"

"So now, I do make some money every year off all the specials," said Barbee. "It's not giant amounts of money, but you know, it's significant. And I look forward to getting that check every year."

Fox News Digital reached out to SAG-AFTRA, Apple and Peanuts Worldwide for comment.

From 1972 to 1974, Barbee voiced several "Peanuts" characters across five different TV specials. Because producers insisted on authentic kids' voices rather than adults imitating children, every young actor received what Barbee called a "Dear John" letter.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"One of the things that's very interesting about all the characters in 'Peanuts' is you got a 'Dear John' letter the moment your voice changed," he told Sibilia.

"They were looking for kids whose voices hadn't changed. They really ... had an idea about the intonation and the character of the voice, and it needed to be a kid's voice. And so, there was an audition. They wanted to do a number of specials at the same time, one after the other. They were talking about Thanksgiving and Easter and others."

"I was about 10 then, maybe a little bit more than 10 years old," Barbee reflected. "And the next thing you know, they had me voice for Charlie Brown and they selected me."

After leaving acting behind, Barbee pivoted to graphic, commercial and site design in the San Francisco Bay Area. In a fitting nod to "Peanuts" creator Charles Schulz, an avid hockey fan who built a famous ice arena in Santa Rosa, Barbee's design work includes the site plan for Fisherman's Wharf's observation wheel and its inaugural seasonal outdoor ice-skating rink. 

For decades, Barbee kept his "Peanuts" past under wraps.

"People that were in the know knew about it," said Barbee. "But many of the people that I've known throughout the years, I never talked about it. It was just not a big thing for me. It was just kind of a funny insider thing. And if you really got to know me, you either found out, maybe I dropped it or a friend mentioned it."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Today, Barbee says the greatest reward is knowing his voice still brings holiday cheer into homes across America half a century later.

"I get this fan mail with frequency still to this day," said Barbee. "And that just always puts a smile on my face because I realize how this character has influenced so many people's lives over the course of, you know, half a century. And there's something very, you know, very special about that. So, it's cool to be involved in that."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers vs Mike McCarthy: Timeline of beloved Super Bowl duo's descent into baffling NFL soap opera
item.description: Aaron Rodgers accused Mike McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings and missing walkthroughs on "The Pat McAfee Show" before the Steelers released him.
