Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy made divorce the theme of this Thanksgiving.

Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings, skipping team activities and harboring resentment over his 2018 firing in Green Bay, even claiming he had covered for his coach for years. McCarthy denied holding a grudge against Rodgers.

But long before their reunion in Pittsburgh imploded, the two men shared a complicated 21-year history that included an NFL Draft rejection, a Super Bowl triumph, public confrontations and seemingly heartfelt reconciliations.

Before Rodgers ever played a snap in the NFL, McCarthy helped deny him a childhood dream.

McCarthy was the San Francisco 49ers' offensive coordinator in 2005 and helped evaluate Rodgers, a Northern California native and lifelong 49ers fan who starred at nearby Cal. But San Francisco selected Utah quarterback Alex Smith with the No. 1 overall pick, leaving Rodgers to endure an infamous, hours-long wait in the NFL Draft green room on national television before Green Bay selected him 24th overall.

Former 49ers head coach Mike Nolan acknowledged McCarthy's influence on the decision in Ian O'Connor's 2024 biography of Rodgers, saying McCarthy was the most knowledgeable member of the group when it came to quarterbacks.

"It was my first head coaching job, and Mike was the guy who was most knowledgeable on quarterbacks of the group, and as a group that's what we decided. … He had a lot to do with picking the other one (Smith), and in the end he got the one (Rodgers) that he didn't pick, and it elevated his career," Nolan said in the book.

McCarthy was quoted in the book giving his side of that story, saying "I was the offensive coordinator, and I did express my opinion. But those selections are made by a group of people, and ultimately a lot of information goes into that. I thought both quarterbacks were very young, talented guys who you could win with."

Three years after passing on Rodgers in the draft, McCarthy publicly admitted he had misjudged the quarterback.

"Aaron is extremely athletic," McCarthy said. "I've said it before, I did not evaluate him properly in the movement phase at quarterback coming out of college. I did not see the athletic ability that I have been able to witness since we've worked together."

McCarthy had spent the previous two seasons developing Rodgers and was preparing him to take over as the Packers' starting quarterback following Brett Favre's retirement.

But when Favre came out of retirement that summer, Rodgers suddenly found himself facing the possibility of having to compete for the job he had waited three years to inherit.

Rodgers was met with boos from some Packers fans during the team's annual Family Night scrimmage on Aug. 3, the night Favre returned to Green Bay.

"They're booing all of us, probably me mostly. So, yeah, I take it personally," Rodgers told reporters that night.

McCarthy met privately with Favre for several hours the following evening. The meeting ran so long that the Packers canceled a scheduled press conference, and a team spokesman said McCarthy had not spoken to Rodgers that day, according to The Washington Post.

But McCarthy ultimately stood by Rodgers, publicly defending the young quarterback amid the controversy.

"He's done everything right to this point, so why would I put him through any more than he needs to go through?" McCarthy told reporters Aug. 5.

Favre was traded to the New York Jets the following day.

Around 2010, Rodgers and McCarthy began meeting privately on Thursday afternoons after practice.

"Some about football, but a lot about life. Lessons, thoughts and dreams," Rodgers recalled in December 2018, shortly after McCarthy was fired.

McCarthy reminisced about those meetings during a 2019 interview with NFL.com, acknowledging how much he missed those conversations. In November 2022, McCarthy revealed how those encounters would typically end.

"And it always ended with a hug and, 'I love ya,'" McCarthy told reporters.

Their partnership reached its pinnacle on Feb. 6, 2011, when the Packers defeated, ironically, the Pittsburgh Steelers 31-25 in Super Bowl XLV.

Rodgers was named Super Bowl MVP the following night. Neither man has won another Super Bowl since.

McCarthy briefly handed his play-calling duties over to Rodgers during the Packers' 2011 regular-season finale against the Detroit Lions.

With Rodgers resting ahead of the playoffs, McCarthy tasked him with calling the offensive plays for backup quarterback Matt Flynn throughout the first half. Flynn went on to set franchise records with 480 passing yards and six touchdown passes in a 45-41 victory.

"He's got a bright future in coaching," McCarthy joked to reporters the following day.

McCarthy expanded Rodgers' play-calling responsibilities in 2012 before scaling them back in 2013, determining he had put too much responsibility on his quarterback.

The tension between Rodgers and McCarthy spilled onto the sideline on national television during a Week 3 game against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Rodgers had been stopped at the 1-yard line on a third-down scramble in the second quarter, prompting the Packers to settle for a field goal. An animated Rodgers confronted McCarthy on the sideline over his play-calling, and Fox's television cameras captured defensive tackle B.J. Raji extending an arm between the two men as they argued.

The Packers went on to squander a 16-point second-half lead, losing 34-30. Rodgers threw multiple interceptions in a regular-season game for the first time in nearly three years.

McCarthy downplayed the confrontation after the game, even suggesting Rodgers' willingness to express his frustration was something he admired about his quarterback.

"He's competitive, man. That's what I love about him. I don't think it's that big of a deal," McCarthy told reporters.

Rodgers confirmed the argument was over play-calling but refused to disclose the specifics of what was said between them.

Two days later, Rodgers addressed the incident again on his ESPN Milwaukee radio show, insisting the two had resolved their disagreement and emphasizing their history of success and mutual respect.

"There's a lot of competitiveness and passion on both sides, and every now and then that passion collides," Rodgers said.

As Rodgers and McCarthy prepared for another playoff run after a 12-4 regular season, some of Rodgers' teammates revealed how intense the relationship between the two men could get behind the scenes.

Former Packers backup quarterback Seneca Wallace told NFL.com that McCarthy would become frustrated when Rodgers independently called plays without his knowledge, sometimes prompting the coach to blurt out, "What the f---? What is he calling?"

Wallace estimated Rodgers could call 40 of the team's 70 offensive plays in a given game.

"Coach McCarthy always talks about alpha dogs — well, they're like two alphas going at it," Packers linebacker and close friend of Rodgers, A.J. Hawk, told NFL.com.

Rodgers suggested their occasional confrontations had only strengthened their relationship.

"But I think we both know each other well enough that the last thing that either of us want to do is disrespect each other," Rodgers said.

Speculation about tension between Rodgers and McCarthy became so widespread among Packers fans that the two agreed to give separate interviews to Green Bay Press-Gazette reporter Pete Dougherty to address their relationship.

The Packers had just finished their worst regular season in total offense since Rodgers became the starting quarterback.

"This is the most frustrated I've ever seen him," McCarthy said of Rodgers.

McCarthy suggested he was uniquely positioned to challenge Rodgers, while the quarterback maintained their disagreements had always been constructive and rooted in mutual respect.

Just two days after the interviews were published, television cameras captured Rodgers and McCarthy sharing playful moments on the sideline during a 35-18 playoff victory over Washington.

McCarthy acknowledged the significance of those images amid the speculation about their relationship.

"I enjoy our relationship. I guess it's good everybody got to see good clips," McCarthy told reporters the following day.

Four years after their heated sideline confrontation in Cincinnati, another game against the Bengals produced an awkward moment between Rodgers and McCarthy.

CBS cameras captured Rodgers looking toward the Packers' sideline and appearing to mouth, "Stupid f---ing call!" twice after taking a sack late in the third quarter.

When Rodgers arrived for his individual meeting with McCarthy the following week, the head coach already had footage of the incident pulled up on a screen, according to a November 2018 Sports Illustrated report.

McCarthy had worked with Rodgers early in his career on controlling his body language when frustrated. More than a decade into their partnership, the two reportedly revisited those lessons.

The Packers ultimately won the game 27-24 in overtime.

Alex Van Pelt, who played quarterback at the University of Pittsburgh while McCarthy was a graduate assistant there, had served as Rodgers' quarterbacks coach since 2014.

But McCarthy brought in a new quarterbacks coach after Van Pelt's contract expired following the 2017 season.

Rodgers publicly expressed his displeasure during an appearance on ESPN Radio's "Golic and Wingo" during Super Bowl week.

"Well, my quarterback coach didn't get retained," Rodgers said. "I thought that was an interesting change, really without consulting me."

McCarthy had previously characterized Van Pelt's departure as a mutual decision, as the assistant had aspirations of becoming an offensive coordinator.

However, several sources close to the Packers later told Sports Illustrated they believed McCarthy had come to view Van Pelt as a threat because of his close relationship with Rodgers.

Van Pelt ultimately took another quarterbacks coaching job with the Cincinnati Bengals.

Rodgers was celebrating his 35th birthday on Dec. 2, 2018, when he learned McCarthy had been fired.

"I was at home with my folks in town for my birthday. When I found out, I was as shocked as many of you were, I'm sure," Rodgers said.

The Packers had fallen to 4-7-1 after an embarrassing 20-17 home loss to the Arizona Cardinals earlier that day, prompting the franchise to abruptly end McCarthy's tenure after nearly 13 seasons.

Fox Sports' Terry Bradshaw suggested Rodgers was responsible for McCarthy's firing, an assertion Packers president Mark Murphy publicly disputed the following day.

Rodgers also pushed back against speculation about their deteriorating relationship, revealing that he and McCarthy had actually spent more time talking to each other during the 2018 season than in previous years.

But it was a chance encounter outside Lambeau Field in the days after the firing that made the separation particularly surreal for Rodgers.

While driving to work one morning, Rodgers looked across an intersection and spotted McCarthy sitting in his truck. Rodgers recounted the encounter to reporters four years later.

"It was a really weird feeling," Rodgers said, recalling the moment it finally sank in that McCarthy was no longer his head coach.

Four months after their separation, an extensive Bleacher Report investigation exposed alleged dysfunction between Rodgers and McCarthy dating back to the early years of their partnership.

The report alleged McCarthy would miss team meetings to receive massages in his office, while Rodgers had privately questioned his coach's football intelligence and harbored resentment dating back to the 2005 NFL Draft.

McCarthy denied the massage allegations, calling them "utterly absurd."

But perhaps McCarthy's most prominent defender was Rodgers himself.

During an April 8 appearance on ESPN Wisconsin's "Wilde and Tausch," Rodgers characterized the report as a "smear attack," defended McCarthy's character and revealed he regretted publicly criticizing his coach's game plan after the Buffalo game the previous September.

"I love Mike McCarthy. He's a great man, he has a huge heart," Rodgers said.

Rodgers also pointed to his decision to sign a four-year, $134 million contract extension in August 2018 as evidence against the notion that he disliked playing for McCarthy, arguing he had anticipated spending the remainder of his career with him.

Rodgers even made a personal plea to Packers fans in Green Bay, where McCarthy and his family still lived.

"If you see Mike, shake his hand. Tell him thanks for the memories. Tell him thanks for the coaching job that he did," Rodgers said.

Four years after their separation, McCarthy returned to Lambeau Field to face Rodgers as opponents for the first time, with McCarthy coaching the Dallas Cowboys.

The two men had been communicating more frequently over the previous year, according to Rodgers, and exchanged compliments publicly in the days leading up to the game.

Television cameras captured Rodgers and McCarthy sharing an embrace during pregame warmups. But Rodgers later revealed the two had arranged a private meeting well before kickoff, away from the cameras.

"We had a really beautiful conversation before the game. Just really thankful for that time," Rodgers told reporters.

Rodgers then led the Packers to a 31-28 overtime victory, overcoming a 14-point fourth-quarter deficit and spoiling McCarthy's return to Green Bay.

After the game, an emotional and visibly frustrated McCarthy was less inclined to discuss the sentimental significance of his homecoming.

"I'm not trying to be rude, (but) I'm humble pied out," McCarthy told reporters.

Rodgers played a role in bringing McCarthy back to the NFL.

Following Mike Tomlin's resignation in January, Rodgers encouraged Steelers general manager Omar Khan to interview McCarthy, later admitting he had not expected the franchise to seriously consider his former coach.

During a March 4 appearance on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show," Rodgers learned that McAfee had also vouched for McCarthy after working with him as a regular guest on the show throughout the 2025 season. McAfee specifically praised McCarthy's preparation and work ethic.

Rodgers agreed with McAfee's assessment and expressed enthusiasm about McCarthy returning to his hometown to coach the Steelers.

Meanwhile, McCarthy returned to Lambeau Field on March 23 for a tribute to former Packers president Bob Harlan. When asked about potentially coaching Rodgers again, McCarthy said, "Yes, it would be a great story."

Rodgers officially re-signed with Pittsburgh on May 18, committing to playing his final NFL season under McCarthy.

Rodgers revealed two days later that sitting in McCarthy's first morning meeting had transported him back to being a 22-year-old quarterback in Green Bay.

"It's like a pinch-me moment," Rodgers said.

However, Rodgers acknowledged that McCarthy had changed aspects of his offense during their eight years apart and indicated there were certain elements of his coach's play-calling terminology he would push back on.

Just six months after describing his reunion with McCarthy as a "pinch-me moment," Rodgers publicly aired grievances against his longtime coach that dated back more than a decade.

The Steelers announced late Tuesday night that Rodgers would be inactive for Friday's game against the Denver Broncos in favor of Mason Rudolph. Rodgers claimed he learned of the decision during a phone conversation with teammate Pat Freiermuth, not from McCarthy himself.

During an explosive appearance on ESPN's "The Pat McAfee Show" the following afternoon, Rodgers accused McCarthy of repeatedly falling asleep in meetings, missing walkthroughs and failing to adequately prepare for games.

Rodgers said one of the breaking points came during halftime of Pittsburgh's 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday, when McCarthy mistakenly broke down the team's huddle by saying, "One, two, three, Packers."

But Rodgers' allegations extended well beyond their brief reunion in Pittsburgh. The quarterback claimed similar issues had persisted throughout much of their time together in Green Bay.

"I covered for him for a lot of years and we worked around it," Rodgers said.

Rodgers also alleged McCarthy had privately expressed resentment over his firing in Green Bay eight years earlier, believing Rodgers was responsible for it.

Ultimately, the relationship came to a head over the same issue that had repeatedly generated friction between the two men over the previous 15 years: play-calling.

Rodgers said he told McCarthy the Steelers would be better off with someone else calling offensive plays and asked to be released if the team was unwilling to make that change.

The Steelers officially released Rodgers on Wednesday afternoon.

McCarthy subsequently told reporters the quarterback had issued an ultimatum that was "clearly out of his job description." He acknowledged the embarrassing halftime incident in Philadelphia but denied harboring a grudge against Rodgers over his departure from Green Bay.

After 21 years, two franchises and a Super Bowl championship together, McCarthy was once again the coach who decided to move forward without Aaron Rodgers.

item.title: UK shields fighter jets, contacts reservists in Cold War-scale push amid Russia threat
item.description: Wes Streeting says the United Kingdom is contacting former service members to update its strategic reserve as Russian sabotage rises across Europe.
item.content:encoded:
The United Kingdom is bolstering its military readiness amid growing threats from Russia, contacting former service members to assess its reserves as the Royal Air Force reportedly strengthens defenses against potential drone attacks.

Britain's Ministry of Defence has written to former service members to verify their contact information and military skills to ensure the country is prepared for a national emergency or potential conflict, Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting confirmed Friday.

The outreach comes as the International Institute for Strategic Studies warned Thursday that suspected Russian-directed sabotage across Europe could trigger a "mass-casualty event."

NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

The think tank found that sabotage incidents rose 16% in the year through September 2026, with Germany and Poland accounting for more than half of the cases. Researchers warned that a major attack could spark calls for retaliation and divide European governments.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," Streeting told BBC Radio 4's "Today" program.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," he said.

Streeting said the government needed updated records of its strategic reserve in case former service members were called upon to respond to a domestic disaster or overseas conflict.

He cited Russian incursions into Polish airspace, suspected Russian-sponsored sabotage across Europe and Iran-linked threats to British military bases.

Last week, a suspected Russian projectile landed in eastern Poland about 60 miles from a British-led military exercise. The incident happened the same day Britain's defense secretary and chief of the air staff visited troops.

INSIDE THE PENTAGON'S DOOMSDAY PLAN TO KEEP AMERICA FIGHTING IF GLOBAL WAR ERUPTS

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks," Streeting said. "Because the more ready we are, the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war. That is my goal. That is the goal of this government."

The Ministry of Defence said in a news release it was contacting thousands of former military personnel this week as part of a drive to "strengthen the UK’s readiness and deliver on recommendations made in the Strategic Defence Review."

"Service Chiefs are writing to members of the Strategic Reserve, asking them to stay connected and update their details, providing Defence with a better understanding of the skills and experience it could draw upon if needed."

"In the coming months, Strategic Reservists will have the opportunity to volunteer for training and exercises, such as the UK’s participation in NATO’s flagship Steadfast Defender next spring."

The outreach marks the first time since the Cold War that Britain's defense ministry has contacted reservists on such a scale to encourage participation in military exercises, according to The Telegraph.

TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE

Meanwhile, Britain's domestic intelligence agency, MI5, and the defense ministry have reportedly warned British companies supplying military equipment to Ukraine that they could be targeted by Russian saboteurs.

The Royal Air Force is strengthening security at military bases, using hardened aircraft shelters and installing anti-drone netting to protect exposed fighter jets, according to The Times.

The measures follow Iranian threats against military bases in England that prompted tighter security and the relocation of U.S. military aircraft.

Suspected drone incursions over European airfields have also heightened concerns about Russian aggression.

"We take the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously and are always adapting to counter any potential threats," a Ministry of Defence spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING

"This includes investing an additional £470 million to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities.

"We have already invested £15 million in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites."

The developments come as President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe, signaling a shift in tone toward the Russian leader, whom he called a friend last week.

Trump said he made the request during a meeting with Putin in China last week, adding that he believed it could help secure a deal to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump's comments came a day after he hosted NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in Florida. The two leaders issued a joint statement urging Russia not to expand its war in Ukraine.

"During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe," Trump said on Truth Social.

item.title: Trump takes on Somali welfare dependency in Thanksgiving message, lays out who should stay in US
item.description: President Donald Trump says only 2% of Minnesota's Somali community should stay, claiming on Truth Social the rest should be thrown out to save the state.
item.content:encoded:
In a lengthy Thanksgiving message on Truth Social Thursday, President Donald Trump praised a small fraction of the Somali community, saying they should be allowed to remain in the United States, while calling for the immediate removal of those receiving government assistance while unemployed.

The holiday post mixed praise for "AMERICAN PATRIOTS" with criticism of the "Radical Far Left" and Minnesota’s Somali community, which Trump has frequently accused of public assistance fraud in the state.

"I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance," Trump wrote in the post. "These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately, thereby saving the Great State of Minnesota, which has no chance if they are allowed to stay."

SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME

Ken Martin, chair of the Democratic National Committee, said Trump was spending the holiday "spewing hatred, attacking immigrants and bragging about his ballroom," saying he should instead be reminded that Thanksgiving is about "gratitude, generosity and community, not bigotry and interior decorating."

"As a proud Minnesotan, let me make something abundantly clear: our Somali American neighbors are part of the fabric of our state," Martin wrote on X. "They are small business owners, teachers, healthcare workers, parents, and hardworking Americans. They contribute far more to the spirit of this country than a man who can’t even get through a Thanksgiving greeting without demonizing an entire community."

"In Minnesota, we pull up another chair at the Thanksgiving table," he added. "Trump apparently would rather deport the people sitting around it."

SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD HAS NEFARIOUS TERRORISM LINKS, TOP AGRICULTURE WATCHDOG WARNS CONGRESS

Trump’s remarks echo ongoing criticism from some Republicans regarding public benefit usage and fraud cases within the community.

During a House Oversight Committee hearing in January, Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, highlighted data on government support programs, noting that 54% of Somali-headed households in Minnesota receive food stamps.

Elsewhere in the post, Trump claimed that "murderers, drug dealers, and criminals" — who he said illegally entered the U.S. from foreign prisons and mental institutions — have largely been deported.

"They are mostly gone now, brought back to their point of origin and, hopefully, living a beautiful and idyllic life, and promising, ideally, never to kill innocent people again," he wrote.

TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE'

"We won’t have to worry about that, because they are GONE — but, Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from Faraway Lands," he added. "We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!"

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also shared a holiday message on social media, with a video focused on opportunities provided by the U.S.

"We know how special this country is. It's the place that gave us freedom. It's a place that gave us opportunity. It's a place that's given our parents, our grandparents, and many of you the chance not just to do well in life, but to leave our children better off than ourselves," Rubio said in the video.

In the attached caption, he added, "Being an American is a gift unlike any ever afforded to any other peoples throughout human history — we have so much to be thankful for. Happy Thanksgiving."

item.title: Kevin Durant dishes on Steelers coach Mike McCarthy’s alleged ice cream snack habits after making NBA history
item.description: Aaron Rodgers was released by the Pittsburgh Steelers one day before Thanksgiving after benching and his Mike McCarthy comments on "The Pat McAfee Show."
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Rodgers’ time with the Pittsburgh Steelers ended abruptly just one day before Thanksgiving. The team cut ties with the veteran quarterback shortly after benching him and following his disparaging comments about coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show" on Wednesday.

Rodgers, who was in his second season with the Steelers, made a series of allegations questioning McCarthy’s focus and work ethic. He claimed the coach had been caught "snoring" during team meetings and recently inadvertently ended a speech with "one, two, three, Packers."

Another allegation came from former Steelers defensive lineman Breiden Fehoko, who claimed that a Steelers player sent him a message reading: "McCarthy has a personal assistant who brings him ice cream sandwiches on demand."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Several sports figures have weighed in on Rodgers’ abrupt departure, with NBA star Kevin Durant among the latest to comment.

"Happy Thanksgiving, hiring a ice cream sandwich assistant for the day, great idea Mike," the Houston Rockets forward wrote on X on Thanksgiving morning.

NEW JERSEY DEVILS MOCK STEELERS COACH MIKE MCCARTHY WITH BRUTAL 'ICE CREAM SANDWICH' JAB

Durant's post surfaced hours after a 3-pointer in the first half of the Rockets game against the Phoenix Suns on Wednesday, made him the fifth NBA player to score 33,000 career points. Houston went to defeat Durant's former team 116-104, with Durant ending the game with 20 points.

McCarthy addressed the allegations raised by Rodgers, telling reporters the team's front office was ""very in tune with everything that goes on in football operations as far as my job responsibility."

Rodgers acknowledged that his time with the Steelers was over, saying, "That ship has sailed."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Mason Rudolph is expected to start when the Black Friday game against the Denver Broncos kicks off. Rodgers suggested he was unaware he wouldn't be the starter going forward until a teammate alerted him.

Steelers owner and president Art Rooney II responded with a show of support for McCarthy, telling the Post-Gazette that he "expects" McCarthy to "be our coach this season, next season and beyond."

The NFL's trade deadline for this season had already passed by the time Rodgers was released, meaning the four-time league MVP will have to go through waivers before another potentially interested team claims him. If Rodgers makes it through waivers unclaimed, he would then be an unrestricted free agent.

The Rockets-Suns game also managed to produce some holiday fireworks, as Durant and Dillon Brooks got wrapped up in a heated verbal back-and-forth. While players jawing back and forth isn't a new phenomenon, the exchange between Durant and Brooks raised eyebrows because it happened during a live play.

Durant untucked his Rockets jersey and pushed his forehead up against Brooks' forehead. Referees whistled for double technical fouls, with Brooks leaving the game due to a technical foul he received a few minutes prior to the confrontation with Durant.

Durant address the confrontation after the game, telling reporters, "I mean, I just love basketball. That simple."

"I love to play ball. I love everything about the game, all the details that add up to winning. I care about that and I don't mind if somebody got a grievance with me. I don't mind addressing it right there in the moment. I'm sure he has some. I said some things that he probably didn't like, and he addressed it right there. And I can respect that as a man. And it didn't get farther than that. But if it does get farther than that, I'll be ready for that, too."

item.title: Amon-Ra St Brown kicks off Thanksgiving with ridiculous one-handed grab, stanky leg celebration
item.description: Amon-Ra St. Brown hauled in a stunning one-handed catch against the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving, then hit the stanky leg dance aimed at Ben Johnson.
item.content:encoded:
Amon-Ra St. Brown came to play on Turkey Day.

The Detroit Lions wide receiver wasted no time in showing off his catching abilities against the Chicago Bears in their Thanksgiving showdown. He was also sure to send a message to the Bears' head coach, Ben Johnson, after the fact.

Barely two minutes into the contest, Detroit quarterback Jared Goff threw a pass to a streaking St. Brown running toward the sideline. Most wideouts wouldn't have been able to haul in the pass, but St. Brown is not like most wideouts, and snagged the football out of the air with just one hand.

TOM BRADY CALLS OUT NFL'S INCREASINGLY ELABORATE TOUCHDOWN CELEBRATIONS: 'LEARN YOUR ASSIGNMENTS'

After making the one-handed snag for a pickup of 27 yards, St. Brown got up off of the turf and did the stanky leg dance, which was undoubtedly a shot at Johnson, who has pulled out the same dance move inside the Bears' locker room following wins this season.

St. Brown ultimately picked up 46 receiving yards on Detroit's opening drive of the game, although the Lions weren't able to find the end zone after his miraculous catch and settled for a 24-yard field goal.

The Bears-Lions matchup in Detroit is serving as the kickoff to one of the best Thanksgiving Day slates in NFL history.

After the 8-2 NFC foes handle their business, the Philadelphia Eagles and Dallas Cowboys match up in an important clash in the lowly NFC East, with both teams holding losing records still somehow alive in the divisional race.

item.title: Sylvester Stallone endured broke, lonely days cleaning lion cages before Henry Winkler changed his life
item.description: Henry Winkler recalls visiting Sylvester Stallone's blacked-out Lexington Avenue apartment, where the future "Rocky" star wrote scripts before fame.
item.content:encoded:
Before Sylvester Stallone became a Hollywood heavyweight, he was a broke, lonely actor living in a cramped New York City walk-up apartment with few friends to lean on — until Henry Winkler came along.

In his memoir, "The Steps," the "Rocky" icon recalls crossing paths with the future "Happy Days" star on the set of 1974's "The Lords of Flatbush." Though Stallone joked they were polar opposites — Winkler, a Yale graduate, and Stallone from "the college of what's the matter [with] you" — the two forged an instant bond.

For Winkler, it didn't take long to see Stallone's fierce determination to make it in Hollywood. It was a drive he witnessed firsthand when he visited his co-star's home on Lexington Avenue for the first time.

SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE

"He was living there with his first wife and their bull mastiff, who had more slobber than the Atlantic Ocean," Winkler recalled to Fox News Digital.

"He painted his windows black so that he would never be bothered by what time of day it was. He wouldn't be influenced by time. Instead, he just wrote and wrote. And from the minute we met on the set of a movie in which we made no money whatsoever, you could see him. You could see his drive. You could see there was something so special, so funny, so articulate coming out of this, 'I'm going to eat you for breakfast.' And it only continued."

"If you listen to Sly Stallone, you quickly realize he's a philosopher," Winkler shared. "You would never put the two together, but it's true. And he's so open. His upbringing would put any man or woman down. It would put them in a corner shaking for the rest of their life. But his motto is 'keep on punching' and it's true. He kept on punching. And it's been an honor to be his friend."

WATCH: SYLVESTER STALLONE REFLECTS ON CHILDHOOD TRAUMA, ‘ROCKY’ AND WHY ‘TRYING’ MATTERS MOST

In his book, Stallone described how Winkler had to "step over a homeless guy while walking up five flights of stairs" just to see his "shabby place and get a glimpse into my world." Instead of being horrified, Winkler was impressed by the library of tattered books and a shelf holding about 15 screenplays. Stallone had been keeping busy writing. 

When Winkler picked up one of Stallone's scripts, he was stunned. Winkler urged Stallone to keep writing.

Stallone told Fox News Digital he never forgot Winkler's kindness and encouragement during a time when hearing "no" was the norm.

"You cannot get two people more different in every aspect," Stallone said with a laugh. "We were, as I wrote, an 'odd couple.' And yet, he gave me such confidence. He's an intellectual, and I didn't think of myself that way. I didn't see myself that way at all. When he saw the writing, he said, 'You wrote all this stuff?' I said, 'It's not good.' He then said, 'That's not the point. You did 15, 15 scripts. It's harder to make it as a writer than an actor. This is impressive.'"

Stallone wrote, "We were an odd couple. He was an intellectual Jewish kid from the Upper West Side who graduated from the Yale School of Drama — the real deal. I had to learn everything the hard way. We were anomalies in each other's lives. To see us together was like watching a zebra hang out with a buffalo. Still, we clicked, because Henry is a genuinely wonderful human being."

item.title: 'One Job Away' campaign is helping SAG-AFTRA members meet work thresholds to keep health insurance
item.description: Actor Cheyenne Jackson’s “One Job Away" campaign helping fellow SAG-AFTRA members meet work thresholds to maintain health insurance
item.content:encoded:
A grassroots social media campaign led by actor and singer Cheyenne Jackson has helped fellow SAG-AFTRA members struggling during declining film and TV production earn enough to keep their union health insurance.

Jackson, known for his roles in "American Horror Story," "30 Rock" and "Glee," launched the "One Job Away" movement on Instagram last month to spotlight fellow performers struggling to earn enough to maintain medical coverage through the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists.

SAG-AFTRA requires members to earn at least $28,000 annually to qualify for health insurance, with four quarterly deadlines for meeting that threshold, depending on when they joined the union.

NEWSOM SAYS FILM TAX INCENTIVES ARE BRINGING HOLLYWOOD HOME BUT INDUSTRY EXPERTS WARN IT MAY BE 'TOO LATE'

For actors working job to job, meeting that requirement has become increasingly difficult as U.S. film and TV production contracts and healthcare costs rise.

"So the success of the project so far at last count is that eight actors have been hired directly and at least 12 to 15 have been pinned or called back or gotten really close," Jackson told Fox News Digital. He described an overwhelming response, including hundreds of direct messages from actors hoping to be featured, many of whom are just a few hundred dollars short of qualifying.

Among them is William Ngo, who was born and raised in Southern California but relocated to Philadelphia after work dried up following the pandemic and the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike. Ngo, whose credits include The CW’s "The Vampire Diaries," HBO Max’s "The Staircase" and Apple’s "Bad Monkey," is just $500 short of qualifying for SAG-AFTRA health insurance.

Actress and stunt performer Marie Gibeault, whose credits include Netflix’s "The Four Seasons" and multiple commercials, is only $800 short of qualifying. Navy veteran, actor and voice-over artist Jonathan Medina needs one guest role to qualify by the end of the year.

ROB RIGGLE SAYS HOLLYWOOD WORK IS DISAPPEARING FROM LA: 'IT'S THE EXCEPTION NOW'

Actor Alejandro Cardenas reached out to thank Jackson after the campaign helped him book a small role that put him over the earnings threshold.

"After Cheyenne posted my picture and info, an executive from Lionsgate and friend of mine immediately called me and set me up into this job so I could make the money needed to reach the minimum to qualify for my health insurance again," Cardenas told Fox News Digital from the set he was working on in New Jersey.

The actors’ profiles share a common thread: dwindling opportunities in Hollywood during fewer scripted television orders, increased cost-cutting and the continued shift of production elsewhere.

TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS

Jackson previously described the industry’s struggles as "systemic" during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter.

"People that have been leads of television shows have worked for years and years and years, and you know their faces, and you know their work. This year, they’re like, ‘What am I going to do?’" he said.

Meanwhile, beginning Jan. 1, quarterly premiums and earnings thresholds are expected to rise by 1%, with additional annual increases of 1% to follow, according to terms negotiated in SAG-AFTRA’s latest contract with streamers and studios.

A petition calling for an audit of the union’s health plan has also gained traction among members.

SAG-AFTRA, which represents approximately 170,000 media professionals worldwide, has faced criticism over the nearly $1.1 million annual salary of its national executive director and chief negotiator, Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, as members struggle financially.

Fox News Digital reached out to SAG-AFTRA’s chief communications and marketing officer, Pamela Greenwalt, for comment. In response, a union representative provided a healthcare fact sheet and a membership termination sheet.

Jackson, who also performs onstage, has expressed a desire to discuss how the system works, noting that actors can have a strong earnings year followed by a lean one that leaves them ineligible for health benefits.

He told Fox News Digital that launching "One Job Away" was a way to pass along the kindness he had received.

Last year, for the first time in his 20-year career, Jackson found himself $6,000 short of meeting the health insurance eligibility requirements. Actress Kathy Bates, who had worked with him on "American Horror Story," arranged for him to have four speaking lines on her CBS series "Matlock." The work was enough to qualify him and his family for coverage.

"I really did nothing," Jackson said of launching "One Job Away." He added that several peers, including actresses Jamie Lee Curtis and Sarah Paulson, have reached out to ask how they can help.

"Just this helping one person makes this worth it," Jackson added, expressing disbelief at the outpouring of love he has received for trying to help.
